title: Second Epilogue — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Biographical historians and historians of individual nations understand this force as a power inherent in heroes and rulers. In their accounts, events happen solely through the will of a Napoleon, an Alexander, or whatever person they happen to be describing. The answers these historians give to the question of what force drives events are satisfying only as long as there is just one historian for each event. But as soon as historians of different nations and perspectives begin describing the same event, the answers they give immediately lose all meaning, because this force is understood by each historian not only differently but often in completely opposite ways.

Writers of universal history who deal with all nations seem to recognize how flawed the specialist historians' view of this force is. They do not see it as a power inherent in heroes and rulers, but as the result of many different forces acting in various directions. In describing a war or the conquest of a people, the universal historian looks for the cause of the event not in the power of any one person, but in the interaction of many persons connected with the event.

According to this view, the power of historical figures—represented as the product of many forces—can no longer be treated as a force that itself produces events. Yet in most cases, universal historians still use the concept of power as a force that independently produces events, treating it as both cause and effect at the same time.

This strange contradiction is not accidental. Not only does it crop up at every turn, but universal historians' accounts are entirely made up of such contradictions. This contradiction arises because, having entered the field of analysis, the universal historians stop halfway.

To find component forces equal to the combined or resultant force, the sum of the components must equal the result. This condition is never met by the universal historians, and so to explain the resultant forces they are forced to admit—in addition to the insufficient components—an unexplained force acting upon the result.

A specialist historian describing the campaign of 1813 or the restoration of the Bourbons plainly asserts that these events were produced by the will of Alexander. But the universal historian Gervinus, refuting this view, tries to prove that the campaign of 1813 and the restoration of the Bourbons were caused not only by Alexander but also by Stein, Metternich, Madame de Stael, Talleyrand, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others. The historian has evidently broken down Alexander's power into its components: Talleyrand, Chateaubriand, and the rest. But the sum of these components—that is, the interaction of Chateaubriand, Talleyrand, Madame de Stael, and the others—obviously does not equal the whole result. The fact that millions of Christian men killed one another and devastated Europe was clearly not caused only by these individuals' activity. And therefore, the universal historian—after having broken down Alexander's power into components and proved them insufficient—must again accept the unexplained force called "power" and recognize it as the influence of great men on events, which is precisely the same thing the specialist historian said.

Peasants who have no clear idea of the cause of rain say, depending on whether they want rain or sunshine: "The wind has blown the clouds away" or "The wind has brought the clouds." In exactly the same way, the universal historians sometimes—when it suits them and fits their theory—say that power is the result of events, and sometimes—when they need to prove something else—say that power produces events.

A third class of historians—the so-called cultural historians—following the path laid down by the universal historians who sometimes accept writers and ladies as forces that produce events—take this force to be something else entirely. They locate it in what is called culture—in intellectual activity.

The cultural historians are perfectly consistent with their predecessors, the universal historians. If historical events can be explained by the fact that certain people treated one another in certain ways, why not explain them by the fact that certain people wrote certain books? Out of the vast number of indicators that accompany every living phenomenon, these historians select the indicator of intellectual activity and declare it to be the cause. But despite all their efforts to prove that the cause of events lies in intellectual activity, only with great reluctance can one agree that there is any connection between intellectual activity and the movement of peoples—and it is quite impossible to admit that intellectual activity guides the actions of people, because phenomena like the brutal murders of the French Revolution, which resulted from preaching about human equality, do not support such a conclusion.

But even granting all the cleverly constructed arguments with which these histories are filled—granting that nations are governed by some undefined force called an "idea"—history's essential question still remains unanswered. To the former power of monarchs and the influence of advisors and other individuals, a new force has now been added: the power of ideas. But how this new force is connected to events—that is, how one particular idea out of the millions of ideas that exist gives rise to a particular event—still needs to be explained.

Undoubtedly some relationship exists between all people who live at the same time, and so it is possible to find connections between the intellectual activity of people and their historical movements, just as connections can be found between the movements of humanity and trade, handicrafts, gardening, or anything else you care to name.

But to say nothing of the intrinsic quality of these cultural histories—which may perhaps be of some use to someone—they are significant because, after seriously and minutely examining various religious, philosophical, and political doctrines as causes of events, every time history has to describe an actual historical event—such as the campaign of 1812—they involuntarily describe it as the result of power, plainly stating that the campaign was the product of Napoleon's will. In saying this, the cultural historians inadvertently contradict themselves, proving that the new force they have invented does not explain events, and that the only way to understand history is through the very power they pretend to reject.
